materials.text: Fields, village buildings and exchange joined farming with other skilled work; no artifact can stand for every resident.

knowledge.text: The site’s name and public account include Wendat authority over how ancestral heritage is presented.

evidence-authority.text: A modern probability plot compares dating models; it is not an ancient drawing or a population graph.

name: Wendat village life: Jean-Baptiste Lainé and the problem of dating
geographicPrecision: Site-area locator in southern Ontario, not the boundary of all Wendat homelands or the location of every later Wendat community.

interval.label: Preferred modeled village range, c.1595–1626 CE
interval.note: Manning and Birch 2022 prefer a model around 1600 over the older c.1500–1530 estimate. These bounds summarize a model, not directly observed foundation and abandonment years. The article describes probability ranges differently in its abstract/body; no single confidence percentage is asserted here.

alternatives.label: Earlier c.1500–1530 attribution relied partly on material styles and scarce European goods; the 2022 analysis prefers a later model.

question: What changes when a village’s date moves by about a century?
summary: A village depended on farming, building and relationships beyond one household. Public Wendat accounts explain that work and its political setting. A modern scientific graph asks a different question: when did this particular community occupy the Jean-Baptiste Lainé site? Its two calendar possibilities should not be mistaken for a century of continuous occupation.

sections.title: A village joined households, fields and relationships
sections.text: The public interpretation places Wendat villages beside fields of corn, squash and beans, with farming alongside fishing, hunting, gathering, trade and diplomacy. These activities needed repeated work, stored knowledge and relationships beyond one house. House construction also required wood for frames and bark for coverings. They do not make all Iroquoian-speaking peoples one nation. Nor does the survival of a decorated pot establish the daily experience or authority of every resident.

citations.locator: Who are the Wendat?; What was uncovered by archaeologists?; Resources; Northern Iroquoian Societies

sections.title: A reclaimed name identifies whose heritage is discussed
sections.text: The museum identifies the site as an ancestral Wendat village and explains its 2011 renaming from Mantle to Jean-Baptiste Lainé, honoring a Wendat veteran. The Nation supplied the opening heritage summaries. Its present public account also connects longhouses with families, clans and shared knowledge. These are attributed explanations of community life; they do not recover the names or experiences of every village resident.

sections.title: Two date clusters do not make a century-long village
sections.text: Manning and Birch show that short-lived plant samples alone can fit calendar positions near either 1500 or 1600 because the calibration curve is not a straight ruler. Figure 2 displays that ambiguity. The two clusters represent alternative calendar placements, not proof of continuous occupation between them. Their fuller analysis uses additional constraints, including wood charcoal, to prefer a range around 1595–1626.

citations.locator: Short-lived samples and Figure 2; Possible Constraints on Site Dating; end Discussion

sections.title: A changed calendar changes the historical question
sections.text: The older estimate used material styles and the scarcity of European goods in its reasoning. The newer placement complicates assumptions about when communities moved and how objects circulated. It does not prove a direct encounter with a particular European visitor. Scientific dating and community interpretation address related questions, but neither reduces a living people to a single archaeological site.

claims.text: The preferred c.1595–1626 range is a modeled placement for an ancestral Wendat village; the earlier c.1500–1530 attribution is retained as a superseded interpretation rather than silently mixed into one span.

deeperReading.title: Household knowledge is more than a point on an axis
deeperReading.text: The present Nation Wendat describes historic longhouses as places joining families and clans through sharing and knowledge transmission. Its public discussion of matrilineal heritage explains membership through the maternal line and describes contemporary political responsibilities. These are the Nation’s own explanations, offered here with attribution rather than turned into an archaeological census. A modeled date can change which neighboring events a researcher considers; it cannot identify who taught a child, assigned a particular task or spoke for a household at this site.

deeperReading.title: Keep the uncertainty attached to the number
deeperReading.text: A village can have a short occupation and still be difficult to place on a calendar. The selected graph shows that distinction. Additional constraints support the authors’ preferred later placement, but the abstract and end Discussion describe its probability bounds differently. The disagreement matters because the model estimates a likely period of occupation; it cannot give the year the first house was built. Other sites require their own dating evidence.

evidenceReading.title: Read a model beside an attributed community account
evidenceReading.introduction: The supplied graph is a modern research figure. The following short source capsules distinguish its observation, the paper’s interpretation and a public community account.

items.label: Two groups of possible calendar placements
items.text: Figure 2 shows short-lived plant-sample models with separated groups near 1500 and 1600. Panel (a) uses an internal sequence. Panel (b) treats the samples as one phase.
items.interpretation: The figure compares alternative placements. It does not count residents, show continuous occupation across the gap or present the paper’s later constrained result.

items.label: A preferred range retains its qualification
items.text: The paper prefers a later placement using further constraints. Its abstract and end Discussion attach different probability descriptions to 1595–1626.
items.interpretation: The existing case preserves the range and the disagreement without claiming exact founding/abandonment years or one settled confidence percentage. The raw models were not rerun for this atlas.

citations.locator: Abstract; Possible Constraints on Site Dating; end Discussion

items.label: A public account explains social relationships
items.text: The Nation’s public family section connects historic longhouses with families, clans and knowledge transmission.
items.interpretation: This is an attributed present account with its own purpose. Neither its public availability nor a licence on a research figure supplies community approval of this atlas or authority over every cultural meaning.

familyActivity.title: Two possibilities, one question
steps: Find panel (b), the smaller right-hand graph. Point to its two separated groups of shaded peaks near 1500 and 1600 on the calendar axis.
Describe one visible difference between two possible calendar placements and an unbroken occupation through all the intervening years.
Read the source capsule. Name the additional kind of evidence the authors use, rather than guessing a population from the height of a peak.
Write one question about household work that the graph cannot answer, and identify the public community account that addresses social relationships.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: this 2022 research figure models dates from short-lived plant remains. Its two calendar possibilities are alternatives. The paper uses additional wood-charcoal constraints to assess the preferred later placement. A separate public Nation Wendat account explains longhouses through families, clans and knowledge transmission. The graph is neither a population count nor a recovered account of one household.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian, Wendat or family approval
review.scope: A source-sized KEEP inquiry joining the unchanged model figure, selected dating text and attributed public accounts of work and social relationships. No new numerical reference phases or media assets.
limitations: The entire original 1595–1626 interval, alternatives, note/precision, identity, coordinates, claims, object order, dimensions and media metadata/pixels remain intact. The abstract 95.4% and end-Discussion 68.3% descriptions are retained as a source difference, not silently reconciled.

Only the listed publisher text sections and existing local Figure 2 pixels were reread. No complete supplement, underlying excavation report, model execution, artifact examination, fresh remote-image byte comparison or independent dating reanalysis supplied.

The museum’s current twelve-sign page differs from its cached six-sign order. Current headings identify the selected passages; the earlier dated scope remains. Modern community interpretation is attributed and does not assign particular residents or offices to the village.

No new geographical study, measured plan, route or numerical historical phase sequence is proposed. Independent specialist/community assessment, real family use, human accessibility/device checks and physical print acceptance remain open.
